outcome: Pavelescu, Pavelescu and Potter (arXiv:2604.03433, submitted April 2026) prove Jørgensen's conjecture for order 13: every simple graph on 13 vertices with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex (and in the latter case is isomorphic to K1 join the icosahedral graph), settling this small-order case via exhaustive computer search. The general conjecture (for all 6-connected K6-minor-free graphs) remains open.
summary: Jørgensen's conjecture (1994/2007) asks whether every 6-vertex-connected K6-minor-free graph is an apex graph. Before the frozen revision date, DeVos, Hegde, Kawarabayashi, Norine, Thomas and Wollan had already proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large graphs (JCTB 2019, two papers), and Pierce (2014) and a 2020 Involve paper had settled small orders up to 12 vertices; all of this predates the window and is background, not a change. Within the window (26 Jan 2024 to present), the only new development found is arXiv:2604.03433, 'New minor minimal non-apex graphs' by Andrei Pavelescu, Elena Pavelescu and Madeline Potter, submitted April 2026. This paper (a) catalogs 339 minor-minimal non-apex (MMNA) graphs — the most complete list to date, up from Pierce's 157 — covering all such graphs with at most 12 vertices or at most 26 edges, and (b) proves that every simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 either contains a K6 minor or is apex (isomorphic to K1 * icosahedron), which settles the order-13 case of Jørgensen's conjecture. This is a case of the problem (a restriction to a specific vertex count and minimum degree), not a resolution of the general conjecture, so status is 'partial' with resolution_direction 'confirmed' (the settled case went the way the conjecture predicts — no counterexample). The method, per the paper's own text (read via the arXiv HTML rendering), is exhaustive computer search: the nauty software for graph generation and isomorphism testing, plus custom Python programs (isapex.py, ismmna.py) built on NetworkX, run on ordinary consumer/workstation hardware (Apple M4 Pro, Mac Mini M2, HP Intel i9), with the order-13-to-17 search taking about 340 hours of compute. No SAT solver, computer-algebra system, or AI/ML system is mentioned anywhere in the abstract, introduction, or methodology section as read. This is classic combinatorial exhaustive search/enumeration, which explicitly does not count as an AI system under the coding rules (§6.2), so ai_role is 'none'. I found no other 2024-2026 developments: no disproof, no counterexample, no progress on the general 6-connected case, and no mention of AI anywhere in the surrounding literature search (Open Problem Garden, the Wikipedia 'Apex graph' article, and general web searches for 2024-2026 progress or counterexamples all came back with nothing beyond this one paper and pre-2024 background).
competing_reading: None substantial. One could argue the ancillary file name 'NewMMNA_code.pdf' or the description of 'custom Python programs' might hide some ML-assisted code generation (e.g., an LLM used to help write isapex.py/ismmna.py), but the paper's own methodology section describes only nauty and NetworkX-based exhaustive search with no authorial statement of AI assistance, so per §6.2 ('the authors' own account') this cannot be coded as assisted or generated.
what_would_settle_it: The full PDF/HTML text of arXiv:2604.03433 (already reviewed via the HTML rendering) plus any acknowledgements section not surfaced by the fetch would confirm there is no hidden AI-tool disclosure; a check of the ancillary 'NewMMNA_code' file would confirm no AI-generated code is credited.

events.what: Pavelescu, Pavelescu and Potter show by exhaustive computer search (nauty + NetworkX) that every simple graph of order 13 with minimum degree 6 has a K6 minor or is apex (K1 join icosahedron), and catalogue 339 MMNA graphs

judgement.doubts: Settling a single vertex count is an exhaustive check of finitely many graphs, the census case of F4, not a restriction settling infinitely many objects; the general conjecture (already known for sufficiently large graphs before 2024 by DeVos et al.) remains open for the intermediate orders. If one reads 'order 13' as a case rather than instances the status would be partial; I judge it instances. No AI involvement.
